# aldo

**Morse trainer with four teaching methods, including Koch**

- **Version recorded:** 0.7.8
- **Categories:** `cw`, `morse-training`
- **Upstream:** <https://www.nongnu.org/aldo/>

## What it does

Teaches Morse four ways: Koch, which introduces two characters at full speed and adds one at a time; blocks, which sends fixed-length groups; callsign practice; and a QSO simulator that sends realistic exchanges. Everything is generated, so the material never repeats.

## Why you would want it

Koch is the method with the best evidence behind it and the one most beginners never meet, because the obvious approach — learn the alphabet slowly, then speed up — produces a plateau that is very hard to leave. Aldo is the shortest route to doing it properly on Linux.

## Before it will work

A sound device. It generates its own audio and needs no radio.

## Install and launch

- **Installed with the profile:** [`morse`](../profiles/morse.md).
- **Install:** `hammunition install aldo --dry-run`, read the plan, then run it without `--dry-run`.
- **Launch:** Its package ships its own commands and application-menu entry; a unit that ships none gets a generated terminal entry (**D-050**). `hammunition status` lists what is installed.
- **The install needs the network to:** your distribution's package archive.

## Offline use

*Not yet documented for this application.* Read “Before it will work” above for what it needs; the install-time network line above is the only offline fact generated from the manifest. Internet, a local network and a radio link are three different things, and this page does not claim any of them works until it says so.

## How it installs

- apt: `aldo`

## Known problems

The Koch mode's defaults start at 20 wpm character speed, which is correct and feels impossible on the first evening. Resist lowering it; lower the effective speed instead. Progress is stored per user, so running it under sudo starts you over in root's home directory.
